hook: SCP-3450 is a badly written Kirby fan fiction on a flash drive, and its second chapter pulls in an original character the reader once invented, casts them as Dedede's top henchman, and has Kirby eat them and copy their powers. It is presented as a junior researcher's abbreviated test log, with each excerpt written in the breathless voice of a child's story. Enjoy the jokes, but keep an eye on the researcher's remarks after each test; that's where the article actually happens. Those remarks eventually get profane.
whyItMatters:
This is a metafiction piece about creativity, using the most ordinary Foundation format there is: one test after another. The comedy of the fan fiction flattening every clever idea into the same fight-eat-copy formula slowly turns into something much less funny.

It also shows the Foundation's institutional side without any villain. The closing memo is polite and even sympathetic, yet it ends a career in the same tidy register the procedures use.
thingsToNotice:
The secondary effect is never laid out in a clinical paragraph; it surfaces in Rivera's own notes as a steady loss of the ability to invent anything new. Rivera starts by digging up a childhood unicorn princess, then designs characters to break the formula: a self-aware author who edits the text (Kirby swallows her and edits the story himself), a Nobel physicist reduced to shouting PROTON, a heat-powered hero, an orc berserker. Every test comes out identical, and her notes shift from curiosity to writer's block to the bitter admission that Larry Plotter was the best she could manage after two weeks.

On the last day there is no excerpt because chapter two is simply empty, and she breaks off mid-sentence, unable to finish a metaphor. The addendum restricting direct access to D-class sits near the top of the file, so a careful reader is warned before the log even begins. The site director's letter cites lack of productivity and problem-solving, mentions amnestics, and closes with a fond goodbye she will not remember.
